summary: Defines CAPWAP, a protocol for centrally controlling and provisioning wireless access points through an Access Controller. It is designed to work with many wireless technologies, with separate binding documents for each. This is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8996.

eli5.summary: One boss computer manages many wifi boxes: it tells them how to set up and keeps them in line. This memo is the standard language they use to talk.

questions: how does capwap manage wireless access points
how does a wtp find an access controller
what is split mac vs local mac
subtitle: How one central controller discovers, secures, configures and tunnels traffic for many wireless access points.

tldr.problem: Wireless access points were managed by manual configuration over HTTP, proprietary Layer 2 schemes or not at all, so centralized wireless networks had no interoperable standard.
tldr.mechanism: CAPWAP lets an Access Controller (AC) manage Wireless Termination Points (WTPs) over IP and UDP. A WTP discovers an AC, sets up a DTLS session, joins, gets configured, and then exchanges control messages and tunneled wireless frames.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that is independent of the radio technology, with each technology described in a separate binding document. It has since been updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5415 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2009. It has been updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8996, so check those updates alongside this text. The IEEE 802.11 binding is defined separately in RFC 5416.

sections.title: Why Centralize Wireless Access Points
sections.content:
RFC 5415 defines the CAPWAP protocol, which lets an Access Controller (AC) manage a collection of Wireless Termination Points (WTPs). A WTP is the box with the radio antenna that connects wireless devices (called stations, or STAs) to the wired network. The protocol is independent of the Layer 2 technology and meets the objectives in RFC 4564.

The RFC says that traditional ways of managing WTPs were manual static configuration via HTTP, proprietary Layer 2 schemes, or nothing at all. It has three goals: centralize authentication and policy enforcement, move higher-level processing off cost-pressured WTPs while the time-critical radio work stays in them, and provide an extensible protocol that is not bound to one wireless technology.

The scope is narrow on purpose. CAPWAP concerns only the interface between a WTP and an AC. Communication between ACs, and between a station and an AC, is outside it.
sections.eli5: Instead of setting up every wifi box by hand, one boss computer does it for all of them. This memo is the rule book for how the boss and the boxes talk.

sections.title: Split MAC, Local MAC and Wireless Bindings
sections.content:
CAPWAP carries two kinds of payload. Control messages are management exchanges between a WTP and an AC. Data messages encapsulate forwarded wireless frames. The two travel over separate UDP ports.

The protocol has two modes. In Split MAC mode, all Layer 2 wireless data and management frames are encapsulated by the WTP and exchanged with the AC. In Local MAC mode, data frames can be locally bridged or tunneled as 802.3 frames, while wireless management frames are processed locally by the WTP and then forwarded to the AC.

To stay technology-neutral, the base protocol relies on bindings. An implementation for a given radio technology MUST follow that technology's binding. At a minimum a binding must provide a Statistics message element, a message element for configuring station information, and a WTP Radio Information message element that advertises the radio types supported. Binding element names start with the technology name. The IEEE 802.11 binding is RFC 5416.
sections.eli5: Some wifi boxes pass everything to the boss to handle, and some handle most things themselves and just report in. Each kind of radio also gets its own add-on rule sheet.

sections.title: From Discovery to Run
sections.content:
A session follows a fixed order. The WTP optionally discovers ACs with a Discovery Request and Response. It then runs a DTLS handshake with the chosen AC, sends a Join Request and gets a Join Response, and exchanges Configuration Status messages. A Change State Event confirms the result, and the pair enter the Run state.

During the DTLS handshake the AC answers the first ClientHello with a HelloVerifyRequest carrying a cookie. The WTP repeats its ClientHello with the cookie. Each side also performs an authorization check on the other's credentials before the DTLS session is established.

In Run, the WTP sends periodic Echo Requests, and either side exchanges event, configuration and station messages as needed. The RFC notes that the example assumes certificate authentication and leaves out error conditions. Discovery is optional: a WTP with a pre-configured AC can skip it.
sections.eli5: A new wifi box first shouts to find a boss, then the two swap secret handshakes, then the box introduces itself, gets its instructions, and from then on they just check in with each other now and then.

sections.title: The Integrated State Machine
sections.content:
CAPWAP defines one state machine used by both the AC and the WTP, coupled to the DTLS state machine through commands (such as DTLSStart, DTLSListen, DTLSAccept, DTLSShutdown) and notifications (such as DTLSEstablished). For every state, only certain messages are valid, and each control message definition names its states.

The WTP talks to a single AC, so it has one instance. The AC uses three threads: a Listener that handles inbound DTLS setup, a Discovery thread that answers Discovery Requests without keeping per-WTP state, and one Service thread per WTP, which the Listener creates when the Authorize state is reached.

If discovery fails after MaxDiscoveries tries, or DTLS setup fails repeatedly, the WTP enters the Sulking state. It must start the SilentInterval timer and ignore received messages. This is meant to reduce the chance of denial-of-service attacks. After the join, the WTP either downloads firmware in Image Data or goes through Configure and Data Check to Run. A Reset leads to DTLS Teardown.
sections.eli5: It is like a board game where each player always stands on one square, and only certain moves are allowed from each square. If a box keeps failing to connect, it has to sit quietly in the corner for a while.

sections.title: Transport, Discovery, Fragmentation and NAT
sections.content:
CAPWAP uses the UDP client/server model, with the WTP as the client. The AC listens on well-known UDP port 5246 for control and 5247 for data, and the WTP can use any port. If the control port is changed, the data port MUST be the next consecutive number. Over IPv4, the UDP checksum in CAPWAP packets MUST be set to zero. Over IPv6, the data channel defaults to UDP-Lite (RFC 3828) with checksum coverage of 8, unless a middlebox or gateway has been discovered.

To find an AC, a WTP sends a Discovery Request to the limited broadcast address 255.255.255.255, the multicast address 224.0.1.140, or an AC's unicast address (for IPv6, the All ACs multicast address). ACs MUST support all three. Other ways to learn AC addresses include DHCP (RFC 5417), DNS SRV records, and AC lists in Discovery Responses.

CAPWAP does its own fragmentation, because firewalls and NAT devices tend to drop IP fragments. The RFC admits this has limits: the 16-bit Fragment ID can wrap and mix up fragments. Implementations SHOULD perform path MTU discovery to avoid fragmentation. Any implementation MUST be able to receive a reassembled message of 4096 bytes.

For NAT, a WTP behind a NAT works easily since it starts all communication. For several WTPs behind one NAT, the Session ID ties each WTP's control and data channels together. If the AC is behind a NAT, the WTP MUST NOT use the AC addresses it is sent if it detects a NAT, and AC load balancing is effectively disabled.
sections.eli5: The wifi box sends its messages through two numbered mailboxes at the boss. Big messages are chopped into pieces so they fit through small doors, and the boss is told how to recognise which pieces belong to which box.

sections.title: The CAPWAP Header
sections.content:
Every CAPWAP packet starts with a preamble: a 4-bit Version (zero for this specification) and a 4-bit Type. Type 0 means a plain CAPWAP header follows; type 1 means a CAPWAP DTLS header, and then a DTLS packet, follows. Only the Discovery Request and Discovery Response are sent without DTLS. Any other clear-text control packet MUST be dropped. All other control messages MUST be protected by DTLS, and protection of data packets is decided by AC policy.

The common CAPWAP Header has these fields after the preamble: HLEN (header length in 4-byte words), RID (radio ID, 1 to 31), WBID (wireless binding ID, such as 1 for IEEE 802.11), and flag bits. T says whether the payload is in the native wireless format or is an 802.3 frame. F and L mark fragments and the last fragment. W and M say whether the optional Wireless Specific Information and Radio MAC Address fields are present. K marks a Data Channel Keep-Alive packet. Then come a 16-bit Fragment ID and a 13-bit Fragment Offset, counted in units of 8 octets.

Reserved bits MUST be set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers. When both a CAPWAP DTLS header and a CAPWAP header are present, the version in both preambles MUST match.
sections.eli5: Each message wears a label up front saying what kind it is, which radio it belongs to, and whether it is one piece of a bigger message and which piece.

sections.title: Control Messages and Reliability
sections.content:
Control messages come in request and response pairs. The control header holds a Message Type, a one-octet Sequence Number, a Message Element Length and a Flags field that MUST be zero. The message type is an IANA Enterprise Number times 256 plus an enterprise-specific number, with zero for the base protocol. Requests have odd values and responses even ones. An unrecognized odd type gets a response with Result Code Unrecognized Request, and an unrecognized even type is ignored.

The payload is a series of message elements in a type-length-value format with 16-bit Type and Length fields. Missing mandatory elements or unrecognized ones cause a failure Result Code when a response carries elements.

CAPWAP turns UDP into a reliable lockstep channel. Only one request may be outstanding at a time. The sender retransmits an unanswered request unchanged, using RetransmitInterval and doubling it on each retry, up to MaxRetransmit. The receiver MUST cache the last response and resend it, re-encrypted, if it sees the same sequence number again, and MUST ignore older requests. Control messages SHOULD use 802.1Q priority 7 and the DSCP CS6 class.
sections.eli5: Every question gets a numbered answer. If no answer comes back, the question is asked again with the same number, so nobody gets confused about which question is which.

sections.title: DTLS Security and Authentication
sections.content:
CAPWAP wraps its traffic in DTLS (RFC 4347), a datagram version of TLS. Control traffic always uses it. The DTLS implementation MUST support TLS session resumption, which is typically used to set up the data channel DTLS session without a full handshake, and MUST use replay detection. DTLS has its own retransmission timers, so timing out an incomplete handshake is up to the CAPWAP WaitDTLS timer.

Peers can authenticate with certificates or pre-shared keys. With certificates, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA MUST be supported. Certificates MUST carry an Extended Key Usage value that distinguishes ACs (id-kp-capwapAC) from WTPs (id-kp-capwapWTP), so an AC can refuse a connection from another AC. Implementations MUST support certificates whose common name is the device's MAC address, and each side MUST authorize the peer's certificate, for example with an access control list.

Pre-shared keys are strongly discouraged. If they are used, each WTP and AC pairing SHOULD have a unique key, keys SHOULD NOT come from user-readable passphrases, and keys SHOULD be updated periodically.
sections.eli5: Before they trust each other, the boss and the box show ID cards. The cards also say whether the holder is a boss or a box, so two bosses cannot pretend to be each other's boxes.

sections.title: Configuration and Firmware Management
sections.content:
A WTP either keeps no configuration and accepts what the AC gives it, or saves non-default values locally. In the Configure state it sends its overrides to the AC in a Configuration Status Request, and the AC replies with its own settings. The AC keeps a copy of each active WTP's configuration, so if an AC fails, the WTP can connect to a new AC and supply its overrides, with no inter-AC communication needed. In Run, the AC can change settings with a Configuration Update Request or reset them with a Clear Configuration Request.

Firmware management is optional. The Join Response carries an Image Identifier naming the software the WTP should run. If the WTP lacks it, it sends an Image Data Request and the AC sends the image in pieces; if it already has the image stored, it can just reset to use it. A download can also be triggered in the Run state while the WTP keeps serving clients, and the WTP resets when told by a Reset Request. The image hash uses MD5 as a basic checksum, since DTLS protects authenticity and integrity.

The WTP reports events such as statistics, decryption errors and duplicate IP addresses in WTP Event Requests, and station-specific policy goes in Station Configuration messages.
sections.eli5: The boss keeps a copy of each box's settings, so if the boss changes, a new boss can still learn them. The boss can also send a box a whole new set of instructions, even while the box is busy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CAPWAP sits between the wireless link layer security (such as IEEE 802.11i) and the AAA system, and DTLS is a link in the chain of trust, so much rests on the security of DTLS. Because no supported cipher suite is authentication-only, protected data cannot be turned into unprotected data, and message authentication stops unprotected records from being turned into protected ones. The RFC notes that a man in the middle can delete records or cause a session timeout, which is a denial of service in any case.

The Session ID is a random 128-bit value. An AC MUST NOT tie decrypted control packets to a WTP session by the Session ID in the packet alone, but by which DTLS session decrypted the packet, or one authenticated WTP could spoof another. Discovery Requests are sent in the clear and can be spoofed, so an AC must not tear down an active DTLS session just because one arrives.

Firmware handling assumes the WTP honestly reports its version, and CAPWAP cannot tell whether a WTP really stores the image. The RFC also warns that using the MAC address in the certificate common name is less than ideal, but there is no URN specification for putting it in SubjectAltName. Finally, there is no congestion control on the data channel, so non-congestion-controlled traffic is recommended not to be tunneled over CAPWAP.
sections.eli5: Everything important is sent in a locked box, and each box has a long random number that is hard to guess. The rules also warn the boss not to believe a stranger who simply says that the wifi box restarted.

fields.desc: CAPWAP version; zero for this specification.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Payload type that follows the UDP header; 0 for a CAPWAP header, 1 for a CAPWAP DTLS header.

fields.desc: Header length in 4-byte words, including optional headers.

fields.desc: Radio ID of the radio concerned, between 1 and 31.

fields.desc: Wireless binding identifier, for example 1 for IEEE 802.11.

fields.desc: Set when this packet is a fragment.

fields.desc: Position of this fragment, in units of 8 octets.

items.label: Discovery Response
items.desc: An AC's answer to a Discovery Request.

items.desc: A WTP asks an AC for service.

items.label: Join Response
items.desc: The AC says whether it will provide service.

items.label: Configuration Status Request
items.desc: The WTP delivers its current configuration.

items.label: Configuration Status Response
items.desc: The AC may override the WTP's configuration.

items.label: Configuration Update Request
items.desc: The AC changes the WTP's configuration in Run.

items.label: WTP Event Request
items.desc: The WTP sends statistics or events.

items.label: Change State Event Request
items.desc: The WTP reports a radio state change or confirms configuration.

items.label: Change State Event Response
items.desc: The AC acknowledges the state change.
